name: Aortic stenosis (syncope)

matching.reasoningTemplate: Exertional syncope with an ejection systolic murmur suggests severe aortic stenosis.

redFlags: Exertional syncope is a red flag

clinicalPearls: The murmur of AS is a crescendo-decrescendo (midsystolic/ejection) murmur, usually loudest in the second right intercostal space and radiating into the carotids; it is the most common midsystolic murmur in adults (Harrison 22e p.328).

Apical transmission of the AS murmur, where it becomes higher-pitched, is common (Gallavardin effect) and may be mistaken for mitral regurgitation; the AS murmur intensifies in the beat following a premature beat and varies directly with cardiac output, whereas the MR murmur stays constant beat-to-beat (Harrison 22e p.328).

Auscultatory features pointing to severe AS include a soft or absent A2, paradoxical splitting of S2, a late-peaking systolic murmur, an apical S4, and (at normal output) a systolic thrill and a grade 4 or louder murmur (Harrison 22e p.328).

An early ejection sound (click) in children/young adults signifies a flexible, noncalcified bicuspid valve and localizes obstruction to the valvular level rather than sub- or supravalvular (Harrison 22e p.328).
Bicuspid aortic valve is one of the most common congenital anomalies and predisposes to both aortic stenosis and aortic regurgitation (Harrison 22e p.1933).

AS can precipitate myocardial ischemia and anginal chest pain even without obstructive coronary atherosclerosis, by creating extreme myocardial oxygen demand with impaired endocardial blood flow (type 2 ischemia mechanism) (Harrison 22e p.285).

Heyde's syndrome is the association of aortic stenosis with bleeding gastrointestinal vascular ectasias (acquired von Willebrand disease); such patients appear to benefit from aortic valve replacement (Harrison 22e p.361).
harrison.pathophysiology: Aortic stenosis is most often caused by gradual progression of valvular calcification of either normal trileaflet or congenitally bicuspid valves, producing fixed left ventricular outflow obstruction. The pressure overload drives left ventricular hypertrophy, which manifests on the ECG as LVH that increases with severity. The combination of increased myocardial oxygen demand and impaired endocardial perfusion can cause ischemia/angina even with normal coronaries. Syncope in AS reflects a structural disorder compromising cardiac output, and inappropriate reflex vasodilation may be provoked by increased ventricular contractility against the fixed obstruction (Harrison 22e p.203-204, 285, 329, 1933).
additionalDifferentials: Aortic sclerosis (focal leaflet thickening/calcification without obstruction; Doppler jet velocity 2.5 m/s or less) can produce a grade 2-3 midsystolic murmur acoustically identical to AS (Harrison 22e p.1908).
Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (subvalvular dynamic outflow obstruction) (Harrison 22e p.328, 1934).
Subaortic membrane (fixed subvalvular obstruction that can mimic valvular AS) (Harrison 22e p.1934).
Pulmonic stenosis (midsystolic murmur, second left interspace) (Harrison 22e p.329).
Atrial septal defect with increased pulmonic flow producing a midsystolic murmur with fixed splitting of S2 (Harrison 22e p.329).
Mitral regurgitation, given the apical Gallavardin transmission of the AS murmur (Harrison 22e p.328).
nonInfectiousMimics: Hyperdynamic flow murmurs without structural disease (fever, thyrotoxicosis, pregnancy, anemia, normal childhood/adolescence) can produce midsystolic murmurs (Harrison 22e p.1908).
additionalInvestigations: Transthoracic echocardiography to assess valve anatomy (tricuspid/bicuspid, leaflet calcification, excursion), stenosis severity, LV size/wall thickness/function, and aortic root and proximal ascending aorta (Harrison 22e p.329, 1933).
Doppler estimation of transvalvular peak velocity and pressure gradient (Harrison 22e p.1933).
Continuity-equation estimation of aortic valve area, the most accurate echo technique, especially when gradients are underestimated by LV dysfunction (Harrison 22e p.1933-1934).
Dobutamine stress echocardiography to evaluate low-flow/low-gradient AS and determine whether the valve can open further (Harrison 22e p.1934).
Cardiac MRI for quantitative assessment of severity (Harrison 22e p.1933).
Carotid pulse examination for parvus et tardus contour (Harrison 22e p.329, 1905).
redFlags: A weak and delayed carotid pulse (pulsus parvus et tardus) indicates severe AS (Harrison 22e p.329, 1905).
Soft or absent A2, paradoxical splitting of S2, late-peaking murmur, and an apical S4 indicate severe AS (Harrison 22e p.328).
A softening AS murmur in the setting of heart failure/low cardiac output is misleading and does not indicate mild disease (Harrison 22e p.328).
Syncope (including reflex/exertional) from AS reflects structural compromise of cardiac output (Harrison 22e p.203-204).
harrison.prognosis: Patients with good left ventricular function can tolerate severe AS for a considerable period, so valve area or gradient alone should not dictate timing of surgery, which remains a clinical decision (Harrison 22e p.1934).
pitfalls: Avoid aggressive preload/afterload reduction: aggressive treatment of cardiac failure with diuretics and/or vasodilators can precipitate orthostatic hypotension in patients with structural disease such as AS (Harrison 22e p.203).
Transvalvular pressure gradients underestimate severity in severe LV dysfunction; rely on valve area by continuity equation (Harrison 22e p.1933-1934).
In low-flow/low-gradient AS the valve may behave stenotic simply because of the low gradient; provocative dobutamine testing is needed to distinguish true severe stenosis (Harrison 22e p.1934).
The carotid parvus-et-tardus sign is less discriminatory in older patients with stiffened arteries (Harrison 22e p.329).
Aortic sclerosis can produce a murmur indistinguishable on auscultation from significant AS (Harrison 22e p.1908).
harrison.severityClassification: Echo: peak instantaneous velocities of 3.0 m/s or higher (often >4.0 m/s) correspond to gradients of ~36 and ~64 mmHg and indicate at least moderate AS; aortic valve area <1.0 cm2 is generally severe and <0.6 cm2 critical (Harrison 22e p.1933-1934). Catheterization: a valve area <1.0 cm2 with a mean gradient >40 mmHg indicates severe AS (Harrison 22e p.1950). Aortic sclerosis (non-obstructive) is defined by a Doppler jet velocity of 2.5 m/s or less (Harrison 22e p.1908).
